To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nectin-like molecule 1/TSLL/SynCAM3 is a neural tissue-specific cell-cell adhesion protein that localizes at non-junctions of presynaptic axon terminals and glial cell processes.

nectin-like molecule 1 (Necl-1) is a neural tissue-specific Ca2+-dependent immunoglobulin superfamily cell-cell adhesion protein that binds to the membrane-associated guanylyl kinase (MAGUK) family of proteins and localizes at non-junctions sites of synapses, axons, and glia cells.

Necl-3, Necl-4 and Necl-5, in addition to Necl-2 and nectins, are novel Ca2+-in dependent immunoglobulin-like adhesion molecules and that they play important roles in the formation and maintenance of cell-cell adhesion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of Necl-2.
the molecular basis of cell-cell recognition in synaptogenesis and neurite fasciculation.
the characterization of Necl-4/RA175, a novel neural cell adhesion molecule.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Necl-3 is a novel neural-tissue-specific immunoglobulin superfamily member which has a potential to bind to membrane-associated guanyate kinase subfamily members and is involved in the formation of synapses and the maintenance of axon bundles.
Necl-2 and Necl-1, which are expressed in the same cells, are both involved in cell-cell adhesion and synaptogenesis, and that Necl-3 is involved in synaptogenesis.
Necl-5 and Necl-1 are both neural-tissue-specific immunoglobulin superfamily cell-cell adhesion proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nectins and Necls form the nectin family of cell-cell adhesion receptors and play a crucial role in cell-cell adhesion and synaptogenesis.
Necl-2 and Necl-1 are involved in the formation of synapses at the presynapses and postsynapses, respectively.
Necl-2 and Necl-1 are both neural tissue-specific Ca2+- independent immunoglobulin-like molecules that bind to nectins and are involved in synapse formation and maintenance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Necl-2 and Necl-1 are the first examples of molecules that have the capacity to form heterophilic cell adhesion complexes with each other and with nectins.
Necl-2 is a neural-tis-sue-specific Ca2+-dependent cell-cell adhesion protein that localizes to the synapse.
Necl-2 and Necl-5, which are expressed on all neurons, have a role in the formation of axon bundles.
